title: Colombia’s 4–3 pause conceals a preference to cut and a minority seeking to bring tightening forward
summary: Four Banco de la República directors voted to keep the policy rate at 12.25% and three voted to raise it by 25 basis points at the October meeting. The Spanish minutes, released on 5 November at 17:32, reveal an unusually significant distinction between a recorded vote and an initial preference. One director who joined the majority had initially advocated a 50-basis-point reduction and switched to secure a majority. The formal vote was four holds and three hikes. Coding the discussion solely by that tally would miss a director who thought the existing degree of tightening could already be costly. The official English translation appeared the following day.

All sides faced an awkward inflation mix. September headline inflation edged up to 6.3%, a little below market expectations. Perishable food, rents and meals away from home contributed to higher inflation in food and services, even as goods and regulated inflation declined. The measure excluding food and regulated prices eased from 6.1% in August to 6.0%. Analysts expected 6.9% inflation in December 2026 and around 4.0% at two years. Inflation expectations inferred from public debt prices rose at short horizons and remained above the 3% target across maturities. Those prices can include compensation for risk and differences in market liquidity. The minutes report the direction of the indicators without isolating those components.

The accompanying capital-markets report makes the maturity distinction measurable. Between 30 September and 23 October, the one-year nominal TES yield fell 6 basis points while the inflation-linked UVR yield fell 72. Reported one-year breakeven inflation rose 66 basis points to 8.10%. At ten years, breakeven fell 27 basis points to 6.24%. The annex also reports monthly averages, which give different changes. These are observations ending before the policy meeting and include compensation for risks. Treating them as the market’s reaction to the vote, or equating the one-year value with an analyst’s inflation forecast, would obscure both the time window and the measure.

The hold voters saw tentative signs that weaker domestic spending was beginning to restrain excess demand. Private and public consumption growth appeared to be slowing. The August activity indicator and manufacturing surveys pointed to weak sectoral performance. An earthquake, dry agricultural conditions and the fading boost from the World Cup and presidential elections complicated the inference. A slowdown caused by the passing of temporary demand boosts carries different implications from lost production that also pushes up prices. With only one month of softer core inflation, the majority wanted to assess persistence and the food, utility and second-round effects of El Niño before tightening further.

The majority contained distinct arguments. Two directors expected significant fiscal consolidation and a moderate minimum-wage adjustment in 2027 to assist disinflation. The director who initially wanted a cut saw energy shortages, weather, fuel and agricultural inputs as supply pressures and doubted the empirical case for a policy response to expectation effects. That director also linked a wider international interest differential to carry trades and peso appreciation. Another thought the cumulative tightening, stronger peso, external changes and prospective fiscal contraction were damaging firms’ expectations. These were individual views, not a collective estimate of currency sensitivity or fiscal multipliers.

The three hike voters wanted to move while they believed demand still exceeded capacity. They argued that a 2027 inflation outcome above staff’s 4.8% projection would undermine credibility and delay convergence in 2028. In their account, the output gap would close in mid-2027 and turn negative thereafter. Waiting could force the Bank to maintain restraint when unemployment was rising and countercyclical easing would otherwise be useful. They also argued that gas import dependence could magnify the food and energy consequences of a strong El Niño relative to past episodes. Robust terms of trade and household income might cushion the earthquake’s effect on output and employment. They attached less weight to interest differentials in explaining peso appreciation than the director who initially favoured a cut.

Fiscal policy connected the two sides. The Board called for careful study of the Economic Recovery Bill before Congress. Some directors anticipated disinflationary effects from fiscal consolidation. The hike voters saw a commitment to the inflation target as complementary to the government’s fiscal strategy. Neither group established that a particular legislative package would pass. The most informative change in the next releases would be persistent improvement in core and services inflation alongside weaker private demand, or evidence that food and energy pressures were already reaching broader price setting. The minutes record disagreement over both outcomes and timing, with no unconditional commitment on the next decision.

questions.question: Would the decline in core inflation survive the composition effects of the earthquake and the second-quarter demand boost?
questions.detail: Compare rents, restaurant services, tradable goods and other core components with consumption and production in more and less affected areas. Distinguish slower year-on-year growth from falling underlying momentum, and track changes across several releases. Broad cooling after temporary events dropped out would lend the hold majority more support than one favourable monthly observation.

questions.question: Did the wider interest differential contribute materially to peso appreciation?
questions.detail: Compare changes in exchange rates around domestic policy surprises with contemporaneous regional currencies, oil prices, risk appetite and country-specific fiscal news. Where available, distinguish changes in carry positions from changes in spot prices. The minutes record opposing interpretations among directors, not evidence of how much appreciation the differential caused. The time of the November minutes release must also be kept distinct from the October rate decision.

questions.question: Could delaying a hike force tighter policy after the output gap turns negative?
questions.detail: Evaluate vintages of output-gap estimates, survey expectations and realised inflation against the hike voters’ mid-2027 timing. Test alternative assumptions for minimum wages, gas imports, El Niño and fiscal consolidation. A cost comparison needs both the future output lost to additional restraint and the inflation persistence avoided by acting earlier. Neither quantity follows directly from the close vote.
